_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Mathematics unit lecture film, Asking and Sorting. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson page's own order and its own survey: the twelve children of CLASS asked which fruit they like best (pineapple 5, banana 4, orange 2, apple 1, twelve altogether), the list and the table of steps 5 and 6, the block graph of steps 7 and 8, the pictogram of step 9, the hoop, Venn and Carroll of steps 10 to 12, and the pet graph of steps 13 and 14 (dog 6, cat 4, fish 4, bird 2).
title: Asking and Sorting
subtitle: Grade 1 Mathematics
objectives: Record, organise and represent categorical data using: practical resources and drawings lists and tables Venn and Carroll diagrams block graphs and pictograms.
Describe data, using familiar language including reference to more, less, most or least to answer non-statistical questions and discuss conclusions.

beats.say: Twelve children. One question. Which fruit do you like best?
You collect every answer, then draw what the class said.
Before you can draw anything, you need answers.
So ask every child the same question, one at a time.
Amina says pineapple. Musa says banana. Hodan says pineapple.
Ask each child once. All twelve answers line up in rows.
A list writes every answer down, one under the other.
Twelve children, so the list is twelve lines long.
To count the pineapples you read down every single line.
A table is shorter. It writes each answer only once.
Pineapple five, banana four, orange two, apple one: twelve children.
A block graph turns those numbers into towers of blocks.
One block means one child, and nothing else at all.
Five children chose pineapple, so its tower is five blocks.
Four blocks for banana, two for orange, one for apple.
Pineapple is the tallest, so most children chose pineapple.
Apple is the shortest. Only one child chose apple.
A pictogram shows the same answers, using little pictures.
One picture stands for one child, every single time.
The banana row has four pictures, so four children chose banana.
Now sort. A hoop holds everything that follows one rule.
Two hoops that cross over make a Venn diagram.
This hoop is for red. That hoop is for circles.
A red circle follows both rules, so it goes in the middle.
A blue triangle follows neither rule, so it stays outside.
A Carroll diagram does the same job, using four boxes.
This graph is about pets. Six have a dog, two a bird.
So more children have a dog than a bird. Point at it.
Cat and fish are both four, so their towers match exactly.
The graph never says dogs are best. It only counts.
You asked everyone once, and wrote every answer down.
A block graph and a pictogram show the very same answers.
Hoops and boxes sort. A graph says what people really said.
